newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria Moslem leader appeals for recognition.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria Moslem leader appeals for recognition.

text.p: One of Bulgaria's rival Moslem leaders appealed to the new cabinet on Wednesday to register his religious council, in a dispute mirroring the split in the country's Orthodox church.
The Supreme Court last week overturned a decision by the previous Socialist government to refuse to register Fikri Sali's High Moslem Council as the country's highest Moslem authority.
"The government...must mend the mistake of the communists and legalise us," Sali told a news conference. "The registration should be made as soon as possible."
Sali said that interim prime minister Stefan Sofianski had promised to discuss the matter with his advisers.
Sali was Chief Mufti from 1992 to November 1994, when a national council elected Nedim Gendjev as head of the High Spiritual Council and appointed a new chief mufti.
In March 1995, more than 1,000 Moslems voted to restore Sali at an extraordinary national conference following allegations that Gendjev had once been a communist agent.
Calling themselves the High Moslem Council, they sought registration from the government, which refused on the grounds that it had already registered a Moslem council.
The Supreme Court said it was returning the registration case for review by the new cabinet.
"There is no question of talks with the current chairman," Sali said, adding that as soon as his Moslem council was registered, a special team would investigate Gendjev's background.
Gendjev was appointed Chief Mufti in 1988, a year before communist ruler Todor Zhivkov was toppled.
During the 1980s, one million ethnic Turks were forced to adopt Bulgarian names and their rights were severely curbed.
At the height of the persecution more than 300,000 Bulgarian ethnic Turks joined an exodus to Turkey in the summer of 1989, although more than half of them have since returned.
Since the collapse of communism Bulgaria's ethnic Turks have had their own newspaper, cultural centres and political representation in parliament.
In a parallel dispute among Bulgaria's Christians, the same court on March 5 declared invalid the registration of one of two rival synods of the Bulgarian Orthodox church.
Patriarch Maxim's opponents say he should be replaced because he was appointed in the Zhivkov era rather than elected but he said he would not resign despite the ruling.
